title: How AI-friendly is Unreal Engine 5.8 compared to Godot when using Claude?
author: Faisal_alwaal
selftext:
Hey guys,

I'm curious about how well Unreal Engine 5.8 works with AI, specifically Claude. Are there any major limitations to what Claude can do within the engine?

I'm currently developing my game in Godot, mainly because Claude can handle pretty much everything on its own, from writing code and implementing features to debugging and managing the project.

I've been considering switching to Unreal Engine, but I'm wondering if Claude would have the same level of control and autonomy as it does with Godot.

For those using Claude or other AI coding agents with Unreal Engine, how has your experience been? Can AI handle most of the development process, including Blueprints, animations, and gameplay systems, or does it still require a lot of manual work in the editor?

comments.author: ChirpXel
comments.body:
Yes lol, actually. Allot of those aspects such as creating the actual animations or models require outside software. 

But once the finished pieces are inside unreal Claude is more than able to build you an animation pipeline, and chain things together cleanly. Same is true for placing objects in the level, core level layout designs, and again I say whatever else you need

replies.author: bustoutanother1000
replies.body: Animations is actually my main pain, any software solutions you would recommend ?

replies.author: Nostradamivre
replies.body: Use Blender and try to find a good rig. Consider buying one if the free one don't fit you.  it helps a lot if you have zero experience in animation.

replies.author: ChirpXel
replies.body:
Blender is fine, Maya is industry standard. 
Motion Capture is a cheat code, if your animating realistic humanoids. 
For good animation, AI needs guidance. At best you can get begginer level animations out of AI without being an animator yourself currently. 

But don't worry, people like me are training it to be a better animator each day, so it's getting better and better little by little lol.

comments.author: Haunting-Frosting417
comments.body:
If you don’t even use the engine itself, why change?

It’s possible, but the answer is NO, it won’t be self sufficient enough, it will eat more tokens too. If your pc isn’t good enough for UE, it will be slower testing things. 

Honestly, the way you’re not using the engines, you could vibe code your own engine for the game and nothing changes.

comments.author: Haunting-Frosting417
comments.body: Yeah, but if Claude is doing all the work, he won’t be using the tools of the engine. So autonomy won’t change anything for OP

replies.author: _HoundOfJustice
replies.body: Then he might just as well stick with Godot.

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body:
That depends on whether UE's feature set provides things you were going to have to build in Godot anyway. For instance if you're trying to make a realistic game in UE, you already have the best lighting, geometry, water simulation, character/expressions, etc that you can get, out of the box, between the engine and plugins available to it. This could end up savings months (or longer) in development time.

Though if you have a weak system, I'd have a hard time recommending UE. With a 5090 the editor opens up in maybe 20 seconds (as opposed to Godot's 1 second or so).  But I've heard of some people taking  5-10 minutes to open up the editor, and yeah that could cut into dev time a lot.

Also it does preclude the use of multiple agents working with your editor simultaneously, because the load on the PC is high enough per instance that it could easily lead to crashes having multiple running in the background at once.

That said, I'd opt for Unity over Godot any day of the week if it's a 3d project we're talking about.

replies.author: azicre
replies.body: so built the game in godot and once it is finished port it to Unreal.

replies.author: CycleMother2006
replies.body: Ports are unfortunately a lot harder than people make them out to be if we're talking a finalized game. You could definitely build part of the game in Godot or Unity and then port it to Unreal though. For instance the game loop itself. But you'd have to avoid touching anything lighting related. And it might be hard to test depending on poly count. For instance I ran into issues with Godot performance just having a couple  million polygons on screen. Whereas with UE, 1-3 million polys is considered fine for even semi prominent assets. So you'd have to use stand-ins for your real assets, too. Which is totally doable. So yeah. Sure, work out your UI,  and graybox the game, make sure the gameplay loop works and is fun, then port all that over and work on your visuals. Actually not a bad idea. Another method is just using the Unreal  API to do quick prototypes completely outside the editor before ever bothering to finalize things in the editor. AI can use it fine, too.

replies.author: azicre
replies.body: the thing is that these people here are in prototype stage anyway. they don't have a game yet. it doesn't matter if the water is genuinely better in Unreal. They don't have a game yet.

replies.author: CycleMother2006
replies.body:
I mean, that's kind of the point of an engine. To build a game. By that argument no one would ever build a game in Unreal because, "They don't have a game yet so they should build it in Godot."

When you go into UE as an afterthought you end up with shit like Oblivion Remastered, trying to work against it rather than with it. If anyone has any thought of using UE, it needs to be done BEFORE they build out any visual systems, or set up physics, or animations, or anything more than grayboxed scenes. Otherwise they're just doubling their work.

replies.author: azicre
replies.body: In the AI age it is best practice to prototype in whatever agents can most easily work with. Frankly prototyping in the easiest medium available has always been best practice. It is just that AI changes the economics here. You can get a lot further than you could before and still quite easily switch over. That is what I am suggesting. Once the concept is proven and you are out of pre-production you can switch to Unreal for production.

comments.author: Nostradamivre
comments.body: What do you mean, Blueprint doesn’t work?? I’m currently using it, and oh Lord, he’s very good at Blueprint. juste need to use some MCP and be on your way

replies.author: Upper-Philosophy2376
replies.body: I'm glad they fixed it then, last time I tried it (like a month ago) I gave up on it and just went al lin on C++, so my view on that is probably outdated, I'll make an edit.

replies.author: Nostradamivre
replies.body:
Yeah, fair point. I think the MCP workaround is only 6 to 8 weeks old at most, so it’s easy to have missed it. It works really well, IF you don’t mind Unreal’s slightly slow code-and-test loop, haha.

But to be fair, the Claude → Unreal → Fab/Blender pipeline (if you’re into Blender) is amazing. It’s a resource hog, but Lord. I’ve been working in Unreal for years and it still blows me away every time it imports my 3D shed and builds the terrain in 40 minutes.

comments.author: MidSerpent
comments.body:
Unreal is extremely AI friendly.  The AI does great with a fully source available engine and the 5.8 MCP gets things done in the engine itself. 

I don’t think the AI is great at editing blueprint scripting, but there’s really no reason for it when it’s much better at C++

replies.author: Luna2442
replies.body: How much do you find yourself editing blueprints though? What about UI? And animations? The stuff that is actually difficult and takes time? Programming is the easy part and Ive never really done a c++ project so im not sure how much you still need to use the visual editor for those things

replies.author: MidSerpent
replies.body:
I was already an engineer working in C++ in unreal before AI. 

I despise blueprint script and only use it for the most basic connective tissue. 

Obviously UI can’t be avoided but AI make terrible Ui anyway. 

I wouldn’t expect an AI to make good animation

replies.author: Luna2442
replies.body: Thats kinda why I didnt bother much with it, I set up the mcp and found myself having the same bottlenecks regardless. It is nice to be able to ask it questions related to your project ofc. My project in 5.7 will probably stay on 5.7 unfortunately

replies.author: alireza_developer_98
replies.body: Agreed on C++ being the sweet spot. Blueprints are binary assets, so agents mostly poke at them through the editor instead of editing them directly, which is why C++ stays the reliable path.

comments.author: alireza_developer_98
comments.body: Claude can't click around the editor either way, it only sees what a tool exposes. Unreal's Python scripting and the C++ source are the real levers, so expect to wire those up first. Godot's plain-text scenes just happen to be easier to feed in.

comments.author: alireza_developer_98
comments.body: The production-grade systems point is the honest one. Claude isn't doing less in Unreal because it's blocked, it's doing less because there's less half-built stuff to fill in.

comments.author: alireza_developer_98
comments.body: The FAB account thing is real and annoying, there's no clean API to list your library. Fastest workaround I've seen is scraping the vault page once and feeding the list to the agent.

replies.author: Upper-Philosophy2376
replies.body: I'm thinking there might be a workaround that nobody has built yet, for example I just found out that people have made their own asset loaders for this, the most interesting has the memorable name 'do nothing and win' and it connects via an API to FAB, so maybe there is a way, but again, nobody has really figured it out yet, at least that I know.
